text: Northbridge Retail's deploy script used to work, until a release directory didn't exist, the cp step failed silently, and the old binary kept running while the team thought they had shipped. Bash does not treat most failures as fatal by default. This lesson fixes that, starting with how to make a script fail loudly instead of limping forward.

Every bash script should start with #!/usr/bin/env bash, which finds bash via PATH instead of assuming it lives at /bin/bash. Right after that: set -euo pipefail. The -e flag exits immediately on any non-zero command, -u treats an unset variable as an error, and pipefail fails a pipeline if any stage in it fails, not just the last one. With those three flags on, a failed cp step stops the script right there, before it reaches systemctl restart or prints a false success message.

Unquoted variables get word-split and glob-expanded by bash. A file named 'release notes oct dot txt', assigned to a variable and passed to rm unquoted, gets split into three separate arguments and deletes the wrong files. Quoted, it is treated as one single argument. Quote every variable expansion unless you have a specific reason not to.

Every command returns an exit code: zero for success, one through two fifty five for failure. That is how cron jobs, CI pipelines, and other scripts know whether to proceed. curl -sf suppresses progress output and makes curl itself return non-zero on an HTTP error. And trap registers a cleanup function that runs on exit no matter how the script ends. Northbridge uses it to guarantee a deploy lock file always gets released, even after a failure.

Shebang, set -euo pipefail, quoted variables, exit codes, and trap. Four habits that turn a script that quietly fails into one that fails loudly. Next up: turning these patterns into reusable functions and a shared library.
